levels.headline: Burnham heads to Brussels for UK-EU reset summit with food, carbon and youth deals expected but fees dispute unresolved
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is attending a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November. It is expected to seal a trade deal cutting red tape for food and drink exports, link the two sides' emissions trading schemes and finalise a youth experience scheme. The outcome had not been reported when this edition was written.
Talks have been held up by two issues. The EU wants students from its member states to pay the same home tuition fees as UK students, and Brussels has tied that to a UK request over the EU's Made in Europe procurement scheme. It was unclear whether both sides could settle these in time.
On 17 November Burnham told the Lord Mayor's Banquet that the Brexit the UK was given has not worked, and said a wider national conversation on the long-term relationship would start soon after the summit. Downing Street says the government is keeping its red lines on the single market, the customs union and freedom of movement.
levels.why: It decides how easily British firms can sell to Europe and how close the UK moves to its biggest trading partner.

levels.headline: UK prime minister goes to Brussels hoping to seal food, carbon and youth deals
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is in Brussels today, Friday 20 November, for a summit with the European Union. Reports say he hopes to agree a deal on food and drink trade, a link between the UK and EU carbon markets and a scheme for young people to work abroad for limited periods. The result was not known when this was written.
Two disputes remain. The EU wants EU students at British universities to pay the lower home fees that UK students pay. Brussels has linked that demand to a British request about the Made in Europe scheme, which favours EU-made goods in public contracts.
Burnham said on 17 November that Brexit has not worked. He said the UK would begin a national conversation about its long-term ties with the EU soon after the summit. The government says it will not rejoin the single market or customs union or bring back free movement.
levels.why: It decides how easily British firms can sell to Europe and how close the UK moves to its biggest trading partner.

levels.headline: Burnham seeks Brussels deals on food, carbon trading and youth work, but fees row remains

levels.headline: Prime minister in Brussels to try to make trade with the EU easier
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is meeting EU leaders in Brussels today. Britain left the European Union in 2020, and this meeting is part of his plan to reset relations. He wants deals to make it easier to sell food and drink to Europe, to link carbon-pricing systems, and to let young people work abroad for a time.
There is a disagreement over university fees. The EU wants European students in Britain to pay the cheaper home fees that British students pay. It has linked this to a British request about the EU's Made in Europe scheme. It is not clear if they will settle it today.

levels.headline: UK and EU leaders meet to try to cut red tape on food and drink

They also want to link their carbon markets, which put a price on pollution, and start a scheme that lets young people work in each other's countries for a short time.
A row over student fees is getting in the way. The EU wants students from its countries to pay the same lower fees as British students at UK universities. It has tied this to a British request about EU rules that favour goods made in Europe.

levels.why: It decides how easily British firms can sell to Europe and how close the UK moves to its biggest trading partner.

levels.headline: Prime minister meets EU leaders to make trade easier
levels.body:
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is in Brussels today to meet leaders of the European Union. Britain left the EU in 2020. Since then, selling food to Europe has meant more forms and checks. He wants to cut that paperwork so shops and farms can trade more easily.
They also want to link their carbon markets. These are systems where companies pay to release pollution. A third plan would let young people work in the UK or the EU for a short time. There is an argument about student fees, and nobody knows yet if it is solved.
Mr Burnham said this week that Brexit has not worked. He says people will be asked to talk about Britain's long-term place in Europe after the summit. His government says it will not rejoin the single market, which lets goods move freely between EU countries.
levels.why: It decides how easily British firms can sell to Europe and how close the UK moves to its biggest trading partner.

levels.headline: Britain's prime minister is talking to the EU about trade
levels.body:
Britain used to be in a group of countries called the European Union, or EU. It left in 2020. Today the prime minister, Andy Burnham, is meeting EU leaders in a city called Brussels. He wants to make it easier for Britain to sell things like food and drink to those countries.
Right now, food that crosses the border needs lots of checks and forms. That costs money and takes time, so prices can go up. He also wants a plan that lets young people work for a short time in other countries, and a plan to share rules about pollution.
There is one big argument. The EU wants students from its countries to pay the same lower university fees as British students. We do not know yet whether they agreed. Mr Burnham says Brexit has not worked well, but he does not plan to rejoin the EU now.
levels.why: It affects the price and choice of food in shops and how easily young people can work abroad.

levels.headline: The UK prime minister is meeting the EU to talk about trade

Today the prime minister, Andy Burnham, is meeting leaders of the European Union in Brussels. The EU is a club of 27 countries in Europe. Britain was once a member but left in 2020. This meeting is about being better friends with them.
He wants British farms and food makers to sell to Europe more easily. At the moment there are lots of forms and checks, which cost money. He also wants a scheme so young people can work in other countries for a while.
They are arguing about university fees. The EU wants its students to pay the same low fees as British students. We do not know the result yet. Mr Burnham says leaving the EU has not worked well, but he says Britain is not going to rejoin.
levels.why: It could change what things cost and the choices that young people have.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe are trying to be better friends
levels.body:
Britain used to belong to a big group of countries in Europe. This group is called the EU. Britain left a few years ago. Now Britain's leader, Andy Burnham, is visiting the EU in a city called Brussels.
He wants to make it easier to sell things like cheese, bread and fish across the sea. Right now there are lots of forms to fill in, and that costs money. Fewer forms could mean cheaper food in shops. He also wants young people to be able to work in other countries for a short time.
They are having a small argument about school and university fees for students. We do not know yet how it ends. Mr Burnham says leaving did not work as well as people hoped, but he is not asking to join again.
levels.why: It could make some food cheaper and help young people try working abroad.

levels.headline: Britain's leader is visiting friends across the sea
levels.body:
Imagine two neighbouring schools that used to share a playground. Then one school built a fence and stopped sharing. Now the head teacher of one school, called Andy Burnham, is visiting the other school to talk. The schools are really countries, Britain and the group of countries in Europe called the EU.
He wants to make it easier to swap things, like food and drink. At the moment there are lots of forms to fill in before anything can cross the fence. He also wants older children to be able to visit and work at the other school for a while.
They have a little argument about how much students should pay. Nobody knows yet how it will end. The head teacher says the fence did not work well, but he does not want to take it all down.
levels.why: It is about being good neighbours, which can make things cheaper and easier for everyone.

levels.headline: S&P 500 falls 2.02% to 7,175.83 for a sixth straight loss as Dow closes below 50,000 on Anthropic debut day
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down on Thursday 19 November, the last completed session. It fell 2.02% to 7,175.83, its sixth decline in a row. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, to 49,097.06, its first close below 50,000 since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to 23,879.20.
Stocks opened higher, with the Nasdaq up as much as 2% earlier in the day, before reversing sharply. The day was also the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic, whose record share sale did not lift the wider market. CNBC described it as failing to revive the artificial intelligence trade.
Investors have been worried about technology shares, especially chip maker Nvidia, and about the prospect of more US interest rate rises. Falling share prices matter beyond the City and Wall Street, because pension funds and savings often hold shares.
levels.why: Share prices affect pensions and savings, and show how confident investors are about the economy.

levels.headline: Anthropic raises $81.3bn in record IPO, closing first day up 17% as wider market falls
levels.body:
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday 19 November. It priced its shares at $83, above the expected range of $70 to $78, and sold about 980 million shares to raise roughly $81.3bn. CNBC reports this is the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX's offering in June.
The shares opened at $111.50, up 34% on the offer price, and reached $115.10 before closing at $97.17, up 17.1%. Estimates of its value vary: about $1.5 trillion at the offer price and about $2 trillion at the opening price.
The listing came as US stocks fell sharply, with the Nasdaq Composite down 2.25%. Several analysts started coverage with bullish ratings and price targets from $125 to $155. Chip maker Nvidia, a major AI stock, has been under pressure.
levels.why: It is the biggest share sale ever, and it shows how much money investors are putting into artificial intelligence.

levels.headline: Budget 2026 leaves £15bn of headroom against fiscal rules, £9bn lower than in March, as debt interest rises
levels.body:
The Office for Budget Responsibility puts the government's headroom against its stability rule at £15bn in 2029-30, according to GOV.UK's Budget 2026 material. That is £9bn lower than in March. The fall reflects higher debt interest linked to the conflict in the Middle East. Headroom is forecast to rise to £22bn in 2030-31.
The government chose to use existing headroom to absorb higher interest costs rather than raise broad-based taxes. Specific measures include a temporary rise in the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, and a lower lifetime limit of £500,000 for Business Asset Disposal Relief.
There are offsetting cuts, including VAT on domestic electricity falling from 5% to 0%. A new Electric Vehicle Excise Duty will help replace falling fuel duty receipts, and salary-sacrificed pension contributions will be capped.
levels.why: It shows how much room the government has to spend or cut taxes without breaking its own borrowing rules.

levels.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first three-way summit in Shenzhen; declaration omits Ukraine and Iran
levels.body:

levels.headline: Commission proposes €45bn Ukraine loan backed by joint borrowing, repayable only if Russia pays reparations
levels.body:
The European Commission proposed on 18 November a new €45bn support loan for Ukraine, funded by joint EU borrowing. About €20bn would go on budget support and €25bn on military purchases. It would cover roughly two-thirds of Ukraine's expected €70bn financing gap next year and be paid out through 2027, on top of the €90bn loan agreed last December.
Ukraine would repay only if Russia pays war reparations, though Brussels says it reserves the right to use around €210bn of immobilised Russian assets. Officials estimate interest costs at €2bn to €2.5bn a year, subsidised by member states.
Leaders must still approve it. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was very confident all 27 states would agree, but Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Bulgaria have said they will not take part, which could stall approval at the next EU summit.
levels.why: It shows how Europe plans to keep funding Ukraine, and who will end up paying.

levels.headline: Government says EU food deal could add £5.1bn to economy as it rejects bacon crisp and marmalade claims
levels.body:
Ahead of the Brussels summit, the UK government published a factsheet and mythbuster on 18 November rejecting claims that closer EU ties will bring new rules for British consumers. It says a food and drink deal could add about £5.1bn to the economy. The summit is expected to focus on cutting red tape for food exports, linking emissions trading schemes and finalising a youth experience scheme.
Ministers said smoky flavours in crisps, sauces and soups will stay on shelves, and British marmalade will not need relabelling because most brands already meet European rules. They said a ban on small ketchup and mayonnaise sachets, or on single-use plastics, is not in the draft agreements.
The government called reports that the UK would pay millions into the EU budget largely speculative, and said the previous government's red lines on the single market, customs union and freedom of movement stay in place. These are the government's own claims, reported by Euronews.
levels.why: It shows what the UK government says a deal with the EU would mean for food, prices and Britain's money.

levels.headline: Brent crude near $92 after November slide as surplus outlook outweighs Iran war risks
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading around $92 a barrel on 20 November, according to Trading Economics. That is near its lowest since late August and down about 15% over the month. Brent settled at $104.77 on 2 November, and prices have fallen nearly 20% so far this month.
The decline reflects expectations of more supply. The International Energy Agency expects the world oil market to return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Middle East exports recover. Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027.
Iran war risks remain. Reports that Donald Trump is weighing further strikes on Iran have not reversed the fall, and US-Iran talks are stalled, with Qatar trying to restart them. Brent is still about 48% higher than a year ago.
